description: Take the Qutb Minar apart piece by piece in 3D, and read the story of Delhi's victory tower: five fluted storeys of red sandstone raised by sultans, and the rust-proof iron pillar in its courtyard.

hotspots.text: The lowest storey mixes angular and rounded flutes; the second goes all rounded, the third all angular. A signature carved in stone, readable from the ground.
hotspots.title: The fluting code

hotspots.text: Bands of Quranic inscriptions in Arabic ring every storey, carved deep into the sandstone eight centuries ago.
hotspots.title: Quranic bands

hotspots.text: A later Nagari inscription calls the tower a victory monument, Vijayastambha. The tower was always propaganda as well as prayer.
hotspots.title: Victory monument

hotspots.text: Five projecting balconies divide the five storeys, each carried on decorated brackets. Firoz Shah Tughlaq rebuilt the top two storeys after lightning struck.
hotspots.title: Five balconies

hotspots.text: 7.02 meters of wrought iron that has barely rusted in 1,600 years. The cavity at its top may once have held a Garuda.
hotspots.title: The rust-proof pillar

hotspots.text: The early-19th-century Mughal-style cupola that replaced the fallen original was removed in 1848 as incongruous. It still sits on the lawns southeast of the tower.
hotspots.title: The rejected cupola

intro: In south Delhi a 72.5-meter tower of red sandstone has announced Muslim rule for 800 years. This is the Qutb Minar, victory monument, minaret, and the centerpiece of India's earliest Islamic complex.
page_title: Qutb Minar: Exploded 3D Model and History | Architectural Atlas

sections.body: Qutb-ud-din Aibak founded the Delhi Sultanate and immediately started building its symbols. In 1199 he began the minar as the tower of the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque and completed the first storey before his death. His successor Iltutmish added three more storeys between 1211 and 1236. Lightning damaged the top, and Firoz Shah Tughlaq replaced the fallen original fourth storey with two new ones in 1368, giving the tower its present five. Sikandar Lodi restored it again in the early 1500s. An inscription calls it what it is: a victory monument.
sections.heading: Eight centuries of sultans

sections.body: The tower is a textbook of early Indo-Islamic architecture. It tapers from 14.32 meters across at the base to 2.75 at the top, and the five storeys are separated by projecting balconies on decorated brackets. The lowest three storeys are red and buff sandstone; the upper two mix marble with sandstone. Each storey carries bands of Quranic inscriptions in Arabic and Nagari, carved so deeply they read from far below. The fluting changes as you climb: alternating angular and rounded on the first storey, rounded alone on the second, angular alone on the third, a deliberate rhythm no visitor can miss.
sections.heading: A textbook in stone

sections.body: The complex around the tower is as important as the tower. The Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque was built with material from 27 demolished Hindu and Jain temples, as its own eastern gate inscription provocatively records, with a high arched prayer-hall screen added in the 14th century. In its courtyard stands the Iron Pillar: 7.02 meters of wrought iron, nearly a meter of it underground, that has resisted corrosion for over 1,600 years, a metallurgical puzzle. Nearby are the Alai Darwaza gateway of 1311 and the tomb of Iltutmish, its interior dense with carvings. UNESCO listed the whole complex in 1993.
sections.heading: The complex around the tower

sections.body: Bollywood has been climbing the minar for decades. The song "Dil Ka Bhanwar Kare Pukar" from Tere Ghar Ke Samne (1963), with Dev Anand and Nutan, was filmed inside the monument itself, in all likelihood the first and last song ever shot inside, before the stairs closed to the public. In Fanaa (2006), Aamir Khan plays a Delhi tour guide and dances through the complex in "Chand Sifarish," giving the 800-year-old stones a very 21st-century close-up. A romantic song from Jannat 2 was filmed at the monument, and the colonial-era travelogue "Delhi" already showed the 238-foot tower of victory to British audiences. For Hindi cinema, the minar is Delhi in a single shot: history you can dance in front of.

timeline.text: Qutb-ud-din Aibak begins the minar and completes the first storey.
Firoz Shah Tughlaq rebuilds the top as two storeys after lightning damage.
The incongruous 19th-century cupola is removed to the lawns.
"Dil Ka Bhanwar Kare Pukar" is filmed inside the monument for Tere Ghar Ke Samne.
UNESCO inscribes the Qutb Minar and its Monuments.
Fanaa films "Chand Sifarish" in the complex.
